title: Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
gist: Outgoing Master of the Rolls Geoffrey Vos, impressed by AI-assisted civil adjudication in Shenzhen, tells Wired that simpler civil disputes will inevitably be decided by AI with consent or legislation, while humans remain for family and complex commercial cases.

insights.claim: England's senior civil judge believes simpler civil cases such as personal injury and low-value professional negligence claims could be adjudicated by AI, producing faster and far cheaper resolution.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Legal-tech and dispute-resolution demand could shift toward automated adjudication of low-value claims.
insights.quote: What most people desperately want in civil disputes is resolution,

insights.claim: Vos was impressed by a court in Shenzhen where civil disputes are decided by judges with heavy AI assistance, and thinks courts globally should consider following.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: China is an operating precedent for AI-assisted judging that others may cite.

insights.claim: Algorithmic decisions will be accepted only if parties consent in a particular case or if society decides through legislation.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Legitimacy and consent, not technology, are the gating factors; watch for enabling legislation.

insights.claim: Vos says explainability concerns are overstated because AI can produce plausible reasoning whose plausibility can be judged, so what matters is outcomes.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Pragmatic stance on black-box models in legal settings; contested by those wanting transparent reasoning.
insights.quote: I don’t think it’s about reasoning; it’s about outcomes.
insights.locator: I suspect part of the reason

insights.claim: Vos expects human judges to remain for custody and family cases and complex commercial cases, though AI will be used to collate information in commercial decisions.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Automation lands first on low-value, high-volume claims.
insights.quote: I don’t think you’ll ever do away with human judges.
insights.locator: Where would you draw the line

insights.claim: Lawyers have been caught citing AI-hallucinated case law, someone in the UK recently lost a license partly through misuse of AI, and chatbot-advised litigants are flooding courts with claims, some bogus.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: AI is raising court caseload and misuse risk, increasing pressure on courts to adopt AI themselves.
insights.locator: That road is littered with pitfalls

insights.claim: Current English guidance advises judges to confine AI use to administrative tasks, and Vos himself uses Microsoft Copilot to find documents and summarize text.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Copilot-style tools are already sanctioned in UK courts at the administrative level.

insights.claim: Vos argues that people will accept an adverse human-delivered ruling over time, but may find it harder to accept an adverse machine decision.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Acceptance risk is a key adoption barrier for automated justice.
